claims.claim: Applied ethics is the branch of ethics that examines the moral permissibility of specific actions and practices, in contrast with normative ethics, which develops general moral principles, and metaethics, which investigates the nature and status of moral claims.

Applied ethics consults normative theories — consequentialist, deontological, and virtue-based — as resources when analyzing concrete cases, and this consultation recurs across applied domains; applying a theory to a case is not mechanical.
Particular cases can test normative theories: philosophers use constructed cases such as the transplant problem as purported counterexamples to views such as simple consequentialism.

Reflective equilibrium is the method of bringing considered moral judgments and candidate general principles into agreement, revising each in light of the other; John Rawls proposed it, most notably in A Theory of Justice (1971).

Applied ethics is organized into domains by practice — bioethics, business ethics, professional ethics (including engineering ethics), and environmental ethics — and working knowledge of a domain requires considerable empirical knowledge, so an expert in one domain may have little to say in another.
Computer and information ethics is a recognized field of applied ethics concerned with computing technology, including questions of professional conduct for computing professionals.

Careful applied-ethics analysis requires reliable facts about the practice as well as moral reasoning: empirical knowledge of a domain is required for serious analysis, and disagreement can persist among careful reasoners over facts, principles, or how considerations are weighed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether applied ethics is best understood as the direct application of normative theory to cases (top-down) or as a more independent mode of moral inquiry
positions: Some philosophers treat applied problems as resolved by applying a general moral theory to the facts of the case
Others hold that applied ethics can proceed with reasons and principles even without a fundamental moral theory, and that cases can in turn pressure and revise theories
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both directions — theories supply resources and cases test theories — without endorsing a single model, and offers reflective equilibrium as a method that accommodates both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether persistent disagreement in applied ethics shows that moral conclusions cannot be justified
positions: Disagreement persists across applied domains even among careful reasoners
Persistent disagreement does not by itself show that no justified conclusion is possible
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that disagreement can persist over facts, principles, or the weighting of considerations, and that analysis can locate and clarify the disagreement without guaranteeing consensus.
